content.text: This convention deals with the correct usage of letter case and symbols. Examples include:

items: Package: Use lowercase letters, separated by dots (.). Example: com.infosys.eta
Class or Interface: Use CamelCase starting with an uppercase letter. Example: String, Integer, Double
Method or Field: Use camelCase starting with a lowercase letter. Example: get, list, noOfItems
Constant Field: Use uppercase letters with underscores. Example: MAX_VALUE
Local Variable: Use short, lowercase names. Example: j, ref, value
Type Parameter: Use single uppercase letters. Example: E, X, T, V, T1, T2

content.text: This convention focuses on the meaning behind the names:

items: Classes should be nouns or noun phrases (e.g., Employee, TransactionProcessor).
Methods and functions should be verbs or verb phrases (e.g., calculateTotal(), processPayment()).
Interfaces should be adjectives (e.g., Readable, Serializable).
Annotations can be any part of speech, as appropriate (e.g., @Override, @Entity).

content.text: These grammatical conventions are more important for classes, interfaces, and methods that are exposed as APIs.

items: Readability: Makes the code easier to read and understand.
Maintainability: Easier to maintain and extend the program in the future.
Avoid Errors: Prevents confusion and minimizes the chances of errors.
Use 4 spaces per indentation level.
Avoid tabs as they are inconsistent across environments.
Leave a space between binary operators (except the dot operator .).
Do not leave space between unary operators and their operands (e.g., ++a, !flag).
Limit lines to 80 characters for better readability.
The opening brace { should be the last character on the line, while the closing brace } should be on the next line by itself.
Break expressions after commas, before operators, and after closing brackets.

content.text: Limiting the scope of variables improves code readability and maintainability. Declare variables as close as possible to their first use. This reduces the chance of errors like variable re-use and makes the code more maintainable.
Prefer using standard Java library classes over writing your own implementations. Libraries such as java.lang, java.util, and java.io are widely used, tested, and efficient.
Instead of writing your own sorting logic, use Java’s built-in Collections.sort().
Never use float or double for precise decimal calculations, especially for monetary values. For exact calculations:

items: Use BigDecimal for precise handling of decimal values.
Use int or long when handling integer-based calculations for monetary values.
Primitives are more efficient than wrapper classes (Integer, Double) because they store only values, while wrapper classes are full-fledged objects.
Auto-boxing and unboxing (introduced in Java 1.5) can introduce subtle bugs if not handled correctly.

content.text: Concatenating strings using the + operator is inefficient because String is immutable, creating a new string object every time. Instead, use StringBuilder.

sections.heading: Don’t Use Strings for Non-Textual Data

content.text: Avoid using String to represent non-textual data like numeric values or booleans. For example, use int instead of String to represent numbers.

items: Use interfaces to abstract away implementation details. This enhances flexibility, as you can swap implementations without changing the code that uses the interface.
Prefer interfaces over abstract classes for most situations, as they allow for more flexible, decoupled design.
Inheritance in Java is single, so abstract classes can limit flexibility.
Interfaces allow classes to adopt multiple behaviors, facilitating mixins (i.e., adding behavior without altering the class hierarchy).

content.text: Immutable classes cannot have their state changed after they are created. This improves safety, especially in multi-threaded applications.

items: Make the class final.
Declare fields as private and final.
Provide only getters; no setters.

content.text: Avoid using hardcoded numbers without explanation in your code. Instead, define them as constants for better clarity.
Avoid cyclic dependencies between packages, as they complicate testing, maintenance, and deployment.
Instead of having a direct dependency between AccountHolder and UserDetails, use an interface to decouple the two.

items: Use the lowest possible access level for class members.
Avoid making instance fields public unless absolutely necessary.
Use final for immutable objects.

Parameter Validation: Always check method parameters before using them.
Constructor Parameter Validation: Ensure constructor parameters are validated to prevent constructing invalid objects.
